Title: Facade: Auto-generating Tactile Interfaces to Appliances
Authors: Anhong Guo; Jeeeun Kim; Xiang 'Anthony' Chen; Tom Yeh; Scott E. Hudson; Jennifer Mankoff; Jeffrey P. Bigham
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the 2017 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '17), pp. 5826-5838
Research area: CV + crowdsourcing + digital fabrication of tactile overlays
Problem addressed: Appliance buttons are flat/unlabelled; hand-made braille labels are hard for blind people to make and memorise.
Target population: Formative: 6 blind women (34-73). Evaluation: 11 blind participants (40-82) on a Hamilton Beach microwave.
Methodology: Blind user photographs appliance with a US dollar bill as fiducial (scale) -> SURF/FLANN/RANSAC rectification -> crowd segments buttons and labels them (majority vote) -> user customises via VoiceOver (braille, embossed letters or symbols; abbreviations; legend) -> OpenJSCAD generates STL -> home or mail-order 3D print -> user aligns and attaches overlay with (removable double-sided) adhesive.
Technology: iOS app, crowdsourcing, OpenJSCAD, FDM (NinjaFlex/SemiFlex/PolyFlex) and SLS prints; base ~0.8 mm.
Main findings: Overlay attachment 117.1 s (2/11 misaligned); braille ID of 25 buttons 98.3% accuracy; locating function buttons 97.3%, ~6.7 s each; simulated cooking 92.5%. Perspective rectification succeeded for 61.8% of app photos. Crowd cost ~$0.15/segmentation, $0.02/label; print ~$10 (FDM).
Limitations: Photo framing by blind users fails often; knobs/curved/very small controls unsupported; capacitive touchscreens disrupted; fixed braille size; printer resolution errors; crowd labelling simulated by experimenter in study; braille-literacy dependence (embossed letters much slower: 218 s for 25 buttons).
Research gaps: Not evaluated on wall switches/switchboards; relies on braille/letters rather than a minimal shape code; relies on crowd; no machine detection confidence or human-AI verification step; not designed for non-braille-literate users or LMIC contexts.
Relevance to SPARSH: THE closest prior work (photo -> auto-generated 3D-printed tactile layer). SPARSH must position itself as an adaptation: Indian modular switchboards (rocker switches + sockets), caregiver-in-the-loop CV with confidence instead of crowd, a 4-symbol functional code instead of braille, and individual removable caps instead of a full overlay.
Design implications: Learn from Facade: alignment is error-prone -> per-switch caps that snap/press onto rocker shape and a numbered guide; use domed rather than cylindrical dots; use flexible materials (TPU-like) for comfort; offer non-braille options.

Title: Markit and Talkit: A Low-Barrier Toolkit to Augment 3D Printed Models with Audio Annotations
Authors: Lei Shi; Yuhang Zhao; Shiri Azenkot
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the 30th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST '17), pp. 493-506
Problem addressed: 3D-printed tactile models alone carry limited information for blind learners; adding audio annotation is hard for non-experts.
Target population: Sighted non-expert makers (authoring) and blind participants (use); counts not verified.
Methodology: Toolkit + user evaluation: Markit lets makers tag model parts with text; blind user prints and uses Talkit, which senses touch with a camera and microphone and speaks annotations.
Technology: 3D printing, computer-vision touch sensing, speech output.
Main findings: Sighted non-experts added ~2 annotations per model in ~275 s on average; blind participants located a specified annotation in ~7 s on average.
Limitations: Camera needed during use; models not appliances; participant numbers not verified here.
Research gaps: Not applied to home controls; requires device during use.
Relevance to SPARSH: Shows a sighted-author / blind-user split workflow (like SPARSH's caregiver/blind-user split), but SPARSH's daily use is device-free.
Design implications: Keep authoring burden for the caregiver low (target minutes, not hours); optional audio legend could be printed as a QR/NFC tag, but caps must work alone.

Title: Designing assistive technology for getting more independence for blind people when performing everyday tasks: an auditory-based tool as a case study
Authors: Barbara Leporini; Michele Rosellini; Nicola Forgione
Journal/conference: Journal of Ambient Intelligence and Humanized Computing, 11(12), 6107-6123
Problem addressed: Blind people cannot tell whether lights are on.
Target population: First prototype: 7 blind + 5 sighted; second: 16 totally blind users; survey of 100 VI respondents (Italy).
Methodology: Iterative design of a 220 V device wired in parallel with a light that beeps when on; user tests and online survey.
Main findings: Task 'is at least one light on?' 100% success; 'which light is on?' 81% (older users struggled); usefulness 4.63/5; 94% of survey respondents wanted a device integrated with lighting.
Limitations: Requires electrical rewiring; on/off only; one home; no stats.
Research gaps: Does not address which switch controls which appliance.
Relevance to SPARSH: Only directly switch/lighting-focused blind-user study found; complementary to SPARSH (status vs identity). Demonstrates real demand among blind users for help with home lighting.
Design implications: SPARSH avoids rewiring (safety, cost) by using removable caps; future work could add light-status feedback.
